export const meta = {
  name: 'nextgen-camera-docs-harvest',
  description: 'Harvest the full Crestron NextGen Cameras documentation set for the i12/i20/p12/p20',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Harvest', detail: 'crawl and save docs.crestron.com area 9440' },
    { title: 'Assess', detail: 'what the full set adds that the VISCA command page alone did not' },
  ],
}

const R = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'
const ROOT = 'https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/9440/Content/Topics/Home.htm'

const GROUND = `
PROJECT: ${R}. The owner supplied the FULL public documentation set for the Crestron 1 Beyond
NextGen cameras (IV-CAM-I12/I20, IV-CAM-P12/P20): ${ROOT}

WHY THIS MATTERS. We hold two real Crestron driver packages for these cameras:
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-i12_i20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.pkg"
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-p12_p20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP.pkg"
Extract either with 'python3 ${R}/tools/pkg_dump.py <path>' or by importing pkg_dump and calling
process_pkg(path) -> dict with 'driver_definition'.

They are Crestron SDK V2 (Entity Model) drivers whose behaviour is almost entirely declarative
JSON, EXCEPT for a handful of Transformations their own Rules invoke but never define. Those exist
only as compiled IL:
  ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles (I20 only), ZoomLevelToPosition, ZoomPositionToLevel,
  ApplyZoomPositionStep, FormatRomVersion, ParseDecimal
A separate experiment is trying to reconstruct these from Crestron's VISCA command reference
(already harvested to ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/) WITHOUT decompiling the IL.

The likeliest weak point of that experiment is the ZOOM family: a command reference gives byte
formats, but ZoomLevelToPosition needs the camera's actual zoom POSITION RANGE, its level scale,
optical/digital boundaries, and any step behaviour — data that typically lives in configuration,
specification or web-interface pages rather than in a protocol command list. This harvest exists to
find that data.

RULES:
- Web access ONLY via the Bright Data CLI: 'brightdata scrape <url>', 'brightdata search "q"'.
  Never WebFetch/WebSearch, never curl to target sites — the owner's home IP must not be used for
  crawling. Report failures; do not fall back to another method.
- Do NOT decompile driver IL. Reading metadata names/attributes is fine.
- Cite the URL for every claim. Never fabricate documentation content. If a page is unreachable,
  list it as missing.
- NEVER submit placeholder or test content.
- FILE WRITES: only under ${R}/reference/crestron-nextgen-cameras/. Do NOT write under
  ${R}/tools/ or ${R}/reference/crestron-visca/ — other work owns those.
`

phase('Harvest')
log('Crawling docs.crestron.com area 9440 (NextGen Cameras)')

const harvest = await agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nYOUR TASK: harvest the complete NextGen Cameras documentation set starting at
${ROOT}, and save it under ${R}/reference/crestron-nextgen-cameras/.

Enumerate pages by scraping the root and following its in-page links, plus
'brightdata search "site:docs.crestron.com 9440 <term>"' with varied terms. MadCap Flare TOC JSON
paths tend to 404 on this host, so do not rely on them. Keep going until repeated searches surface
nothing new, and say what convergence signal you used.

Save each page as markdown, mirroring the site's topic folders, each file starting with a
'Source: <url>' line. Write an INDEX.md listing every page and its URL.

Then write three focused digests, because these are what the rest of the project needs:

1. ZOOM.md — EVERYTHING about zoom: position ranges and their units, zoom level vs zoom position,
   optical vs digital boundaries, field-of-view relationships, step behaviour, any table or
   formula, and any worked example. Quote verbatim with the source URL. This is the highest-value
   output of the whole harvest; if the data exists anywhere in the set, find it.

2. MODELS.md — the model lineup and what differs between I12/I20 and P12/P20: sensor, optical zoom
   range, PTZ vs fixed, auto-tracking features, and anything explaining why the I20 driver has a
   ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles transformation the P20 driver lacks.

3. CONTROL.md — every control surface documented: VISCA over IP and its port, any REST/HTTP API,
   the web interface, Crestron Home integration, and any authentication or pairing requirement.
   Note anything the cameras expose that a driver could use but the two shipped drivers do not.

Report: pages fetched, pages that failed, whether the set covers the I20 and P20 specifically, and
a blunt assessment of whether ZOOM.md actually contains the numbers needed to pin down
ZoomLevelToPosition — say plainly if it does not.`,
  { label: 'harvest:nextgen-cameras', phase: 'Harvest', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
)

phase('Assess')
const assessment = await agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nThe full documentation set has been harvested to ${R}/reference/crestron-nextgen-cameras/.
Harvest report:\n\n${harvest}\n\n---\n\nYOUR TASK: assess what this fuller set adds, and re-attempt
the zoom reconstruction specifically.

1. Read the harvested docs, especially ZOOM.md, MODELS.md and CONTROL.md.
2. Extract both camera drivers' JSON with pkg_dump. Find every Rule and Command that invokes
   ZoomLevelToPosition, ZoomPositionToLevel or ApplyZoomPositionStep. Establish precisely what
   input each receives and what its output feeds into — the surrounding declarative data constrains
   these transformations even though their bodies are compiled.
3. Using ONLY the documentation plus that declarative context, attempt to specify each of the three
   zoom transformations: a precise natural-language definition plus a reference Python
   implementation.
4. TEST each reconstruction against the drivers' own data — if a Command template shows literal
   bytes around the transformation's output, your implementation must produce something consistent
   with them. Show the worked check.
5. Rate each: CONFIDENT (docs plus JSON pin it exactly), PLAUSIBLE (consistent but
   under-determined), or FAILED. Prefer PLAUSIBLE over CONFIDENT wherever an alternative
   implementation would fit the same evidence — actively try to construct such an alternative, and
   if you succeed, that is a downgrade.

A reconstruction that looks right and is wrong would make a driver send subtly incorrect bytes,
which is this project's worst failure mode. An honest FAILED with a clear statement of what would
settle it is a better result than a confident guess.

Also state whether the fuller documentation set changes the earlier finding that documentation
cannot substitute for a shipped driver, or reinforces it.

Prose with headings, cite URLs and JSON paths, no padding.`,
  { label: 'assess:zoom-reconstruction', phase: 'Assess', model: 'opus', effort: 'high' }
)

return { harvest, assessment }

result.harvest:
Everything is in order. Final report:

## Harvest report

**Location:** `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/reference/crestron-nextgen-cameras/`
- `INDEX.md` — index of all 71 pages with URLs and discovery-method notes
- `pages/Topics/...` — 71 markdown pages, each starting with `Source: <url>`, folder structure mirroring the site
- `ZOOM.md`, `MODELS.md`, `CONTROL.md` — the three digests
- `_harvest_meta/` — scripts, raw HTML/markdown caches, intermediate URL lists (provenance only, not deliverable content)

**Pages fetched:** 71/71, zero failures on either the HTML discovery pass or the markdown save pass.

**Pages that failed:** none.

**Discovery method / convergence:** The root page (`Content/Topics/Home.htm`) only links (via `onclick="location.href=..."`) to 5 landing-page stubs (Features, Specifications, Installation, Configuration, Resources), and those stubs' MiniToc child-topic lists are populated client-side from a TOC data file, not present in the static fetch — so in-page-link crawling dead-ended at 6 pages. I switched to `brightdata search "site:docs.crestron.com 9440 <term>"` across two rounds: round 1 (59 varied terms) found 71 unique pages; round 2 (68 further, thematically different terms — sensor size, HDMI/USB/PoE, HDR, tracking algorithm, glossary, etc.) found 57 unique pages, all of which were already in round 1's set (`comm -13` produced zero new URLs). Two large, differently-themed term sweeps converging on the same page set, with the second finding a strict subset, is the convergence signal used to stop.

**Coverage of I20 and P20 specifically:** Yes — dedicated Specs and Features pages exist for all four target models (I12, I20, P12, P20), plus their TAA-compliant "-GV-B" government variants, plus the adjacent (non-target) I12D-B dual-PTZ model that shares Configuration pages with the targets.

**Blunt assessment of ZOOM.md vs. `ZoomLevelToPosition`:** Partial success, and it's the best finding of the harvest. The VISCA Commands page publishes Crestron's own verbatim lookup table mapping integer optical zoom ratio (1x–12x, or 1x–20x) to the 16-bit VISCA "Zoom Position" value, in two variants keyed exactly to the two zoom-range families (12x for I12/P12, 20x for I20/P20). That confirms the position range (`0x0000`–`0x4000`), that it's optical-only (no digital zoom is mentioned anywhere in the 71 pages), and gives per-model FOV/focal-length data. **What it does not give: any formula or interpolation rule.** Only 12 or 20 discrete integer-ratio points are published, with non-linear (compressive toward tele) spacing between them and no stated rounding/interpolation method for intermediate positions or fractional zoom levels. So: if `ZoomLevelToPosition` only ever needs to hit these exact integer-ratio presets, this data fully pins it down; if it needs continuous/fractional zoom, the reconstruction is necessarily an approximation beyond what Crestron publishes — say so plainly rather than claiming full closure.
result.assessment:
## What the fuller doc set actually adds

Three things of substance, and one correction to the harvest's own digest.

**1. The optical anchor table is real and exact.** `https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/9440/Content/Topics/NextGenCameras/Configuration/VISCA-Commands.htm` publishes the 12-row (12x) and 20-row (20x) zoom-ratio → 16-bit Zoom Position tables. These are the standard Sony FCB block tables, and the driver's own constant `16384` (`0x4000`) appears four times as the optical ceiling: `Conditions[…]` named `ZoomLevelIsLessThanOrEqualToOpticalZoomMax`, `ZoomLevelIsGreaterThanOpticalZoomMax`, `ZoomPositionIsLessThanOpticalZoomMax`, `ZoomPositionIsGreaterThanOrEqualToOpticalZoomMax` (I20.json lines 2093–2127; P20.json 1969–2003). Model→table binding is confirmed by `Rules[30] FeedbackForZoomAndFocusRanges12` / `Rules[31] FeedbackForZoomAndFocusRanges20`, gated on `ModelIsP12OrI12` / `ModelIsP20OrI20`.

**2. ZOOM.md is wrong that no digital zoom is documented — and the missing piece was in the harvest all along.** `https://docs.crestron.com/en-us/9440/Content/Topics/NextGenCameras/Configuration/On-Screen-Display(OSD)-Menu.htm` (harvested at `pages/Topics/NextGenCameras/Configuration/On-Screen-Display(OSD)-Menu.md:291-301`) documents, for all IV-CAM models except the I12D-B: "Digital Zoom — Off/On" and "Limit — x1 - x16 — Adjust the Digital Zoom limit." This matters enormously, because the driver's `Controllers[35] ZoomPosition` (I20.json) declares `Max: 31424` = `0x7AC0`, i.e. the Sony optical+digital extended range, and `Controllers[37] ZoomLevel` declares `Min 1.0, Max 320.0, Step 0.1`. `320 = 20 × 16` — optical max × documented digital limit. So `ZoomLevel` is **total** zoom ratio, not optical, and `ZoomPositionToLevel` must cover 16385–31424 as well.

**3. The FOV path is fully declarative and gives a free, independent calibration curve** — `Controllers[34] FieldOfViewConstants` holds four 8-term polynomials (`ZoomPositionToFieldOfViewPolyP12/P20`, `FieldOfViewToZoomPositionPolyP12/P20`). I verified them: they round-trip against each other to within ±5 counts over 0–14000 (`pos 10000 → 14.6830° → 10001.71`), and `ZoomPositionToFieldOfViewPolyP20` evaluates at position 0 to exactly `56.69646700591978`, the declared `ReportedFieldOfView.Max`. **But the documentation says 56.45° (I20Specs.htm/P20Specs.htm) and 67.68° (I12Specs.htm/P12Specs.htm), while the driver uses 56.6965° and 67.0709°.** A doc-only rebuild of the FOV feature would be wrong by 0.25° and 0.61° at the wide end.

## What the declarative JSON pins down about the three transformations

Call sites (identical indices in both packages):

| Path | Inputs | Output feeds |
|---|---|---|
| `Rules[20] SetZoomPositionFromLevel` | `ZoomLevelToPosition({ZoomLevel after RoundToTenths}, {Model})` then `ApplyZoomPositionStep(…, {Model}, "Set")` | `States.ZoomPosition` → `Commands[37] SetZoomPosition` |
| `Rules[21] SetZoomPositionToOpticalZoomMax` | same pair | output discarded; state hardcoded `16384` |
| `Rules[22] ProcessZoomPositionIncrement` | `Sum({ZoomLevel},{ZoomLevel.Step})` → `ZoomLevelToPosition` → `ApplyZoomPositionStep(…,"Increment")` | `States.ZoomPosition` |
| `Rules[23] ProcessZoomPositionDecrement` | `Subtract` → `ZoomLevelToPosition` → `ApplyZoomPositionStep(…,"Decrement")` | `States.ZoomPosition` |
| `Rules[26] FeedbackForZoomLevel` | `ZoomPositionToLevel({ZoomPosition},{Model})` | `States.ZoomLevel` (unrounded) |
| `Rules[27] FeedbackForReportedZoomLevel…` | `ZoomPositionToLevel({ZoomPositionPollingOnly},{Model})` then `RoundToTenths` | `ReportedZoomLevel` → entity property `imageZoom:level` |
| `Controllers[10] FieldOfView.ToDeviceTransformations` | `FieldOfViewToZoomPosition` → `RoundToInt` → `ApplyZoomPositionStep(…,"Set")` | `Commands[38] SetFieldOfView` |

Derived constraints:

- `ZoomLevelToPosition` returns a value comparable to `16384` and must **exceed** it for over-range levels, otherwise `Rules[21]` is unreachable dead code that Crestron nonetheless wrote. So it extrapolates past the tele end rather than clamping.
- By the same argument `ApplyZoomPositionStep` does **not** clamp to `16384` — it runs before the condition is evaluated in `Rules[20]/[21]`, and clamping would kill `Rules[21]`.
- `ApplyZoomPositionStep` is not merely `RoundToInt`: in `Controllers[10]` it is applied *after* `RoundToInt`, so it does something else.
- Increment/decrement never reach it in the digital range: `Rules[22]/[23]` are gated on `ZoomPosition < 16384`; at or above that, `Rules[24]/[25]` send `ZoomIn`/`ZoomOut` + `ZoomStop` jog pulses instead. All position arithmetic is optical-only.
- `Commands[37] SetZoomPosition` template is `"{:hex} 04 47 {ZoomSpeedHex} {Y4} {Y3} {Y2} {Y1}"` with `ViscaExtractNibbles` producing Y1=LSN. That is the doc's `8x 01 04 47 0t 0p 0q 0r 0s FF` "Absolute Position" form, MSN first.

## The reconstructions

Reference implementation saved at `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/reference/crestron-nextgen-cameras/zoom-reconstruction/zoom_reference.py`.

### ZoomLevelToPosition(level, model)

Definition: select the model's published table (12x for I12/P12, 20x for I20/P20); clamp levels ≤1 to position 0; for levels inside the table, piecewise-**linear** interpolation in *level* between bracketing rows; for levels above the top row, linear extrapolation on the final segment's slope; round to nearest integer.

```python
def zoom_level_to_position(level, model):
    levels, positions = TABLES[model]          # LEV_20=[1..20], POS_20=[0x0000,0x1851,...,0x4000]
    if level <= levels[0]:
        return positions[0]
    for i in range(len(levels) - 1):
        if level <= levels[i + 1]:
            f = (level - levels[i]) / (levels[i + 1] - levels[i])
            return int(round(positions[i] + f * (positions[i + 1] - positions[i])))
    f = (level - levels[-2]) / (levels[-1] - levels[-2])
    return int(round(positions[-2] + f * (positions[-1] - positions[-2])))
```

**Worked check.** All 20 rows of the 20x table and all 12 of the 12x table reproduce exactly (`level 2.0 → 6225 = 0x1851`, `level 19.0 → 16314 = 0x3FBA`, `level 20.0 → 16384 = 0x4000`). Rule routing: `P20 level 20.0 → 16384` → `Rules[20]`; `20.1 → 16391` and `25.0 → 16734` → `Rules[21]`, which is exactly the partition the two mutually exclusive rules require. Byte check against the VISCA-Commands.htm packet format, address 1, speed 3:

```
level  1.0  pos 0x0000  81 01 04 47 03 00 00 00 00 FF
level  5.0  pos 0x2D45  81 01 04 47 03 02 0D 04 05 FF
level 20.0  pos 0x4000  81 01 04 47 03 04 00 00 00 FF
```
Nibbles `p q r s` = `2 D 4 5` for `0x2D45` — consistent with the doc's `0p 0q 0r 0s` and with `{Y4}{Y3}{Y2}{Y1}`.

**Alternative that fits the same evidence (the downgrade).** Interpolating linearly in `log(level)` instead of in `level` hits every one of the 20 published anchors exactly and differs by up to **532 counts** at level 1.4 (2490 vs 3022); interpolating in `-1/level` also hits every anchor and differs by up to **1067 counts** (6.5% of full optical travel). Nothing in the docs or the JSON discriminates. Rounding mode (`round`/`floor`/banker's) is likewise free, worth ±1 count.

**Rating: PLAUSIBLE for the 20x family (I20/P20). FAILED for the 12x family (I12/P12).** The 12x failure is concrete, not hypothetical: `Rules[30]` sets `ZoomLevel.Max = 188.8` for `ModelIsP12OrI12` while `Rules[31]` sets `320.0` for the 20x family. With the documented digital limit of ×16, `320 = 20 × 16` exactly, but `188.8 = 11.8 × 16`, not `12 × 16 = 192`. Either the driver's 12x level scale tops out at 11.8x (contradicting both the spec pages' "Optical Zoom 12x" and the table's `12x → 0x4000`), or the 12x family's digital multiplier is 15.7333 rather than 16. The two families' scales are in the exact ratio 11.8 : 20, which is not reproducible from anything Crestron publishes. Under my implementation `level 11.8 → 16319` and `level 12.0 → 16384`; if the driver's array tops at 11.8, both are wrong bytes.

### ZoomPositionToLevel(position, model)

Definition: inverse piecewise-linear interpolation of the same table over 0–16384; positions above 16384 are the digital range and are undefined.

```python
def zoom_position_to_level(position, model):
    levels, positions = TABLES[model]
    if position <= positions[0]:
        return levels[0]
    if position > 16384:
        raise NotImplementedError("digital-zoom range 16385..31424 is undocumented")
    for i in range(len(positions) - 1):
        if position <= positions[i + 1]:
            f = (position - positions[i]) / (positions[i + 1] - positions[i])
            return levels[i] + f * (levels[i + 1] - levels[i])
    return levels[-1]
```

**Worked check.** Round-trip on the optical range: `3.5 → 9690 → 3.5000`, `12.7 → 15353 → 12.7011`, `19.9 → 16377 → 19.9000`. The residual is the integer rounding of the position, and `RoundToTenths` in `Rules[27]` absorbs it — consistent with why Crestron put `RoundToTenths` there.

**Rating: FAILED.** The optical branch is as good as `ZoomLevelToPosition` (PLAUSIBLE), but this transform's declared input domain is `Controllers[35] ZoomPosition.Info.Max = 31424`, and it is the *only* path that produces `ReportedZoomLevel` / `imageZoom:level` feedback. For positions 16385–31424 — reachable whenever Digital Zoom is On in the OSD — the documentation supplies zero interior anchors, and the single endpoint it would supply (`31424 → 12 × 16 = 192` for the 12x family) is contradicted by the driver's own `188.8`. A transform that is right for two-thirds of its domain and silently wrong for the rest is a failure for driver-conversion purposes.

### ApplyZoomPositionStep(position, model, mode)

**Rating: FAILED.** The 71-page set contains no zoom-position granularity of any kind. The only step-like quantities published are the `0(Low)–7(High)` zoom *speed* parameter and `t: speed 0-7`, neither of which is this. The declarative JSON tells us only: it is model-dependent, it has three modes (`"Set"`, `"Increment"`, `"Decrement"`), it maps position→position, it is not a clamp to 16384, and it is not plain rounding-to-int. I can write four different implementations (snap to a grid; enforce a minimum delta from current position; clamp to a per-model min only; no-op) that are all consistent with every observable in both packages. There is nothing to test against and no worked check to show. I am not going to guess a formula that decides what bytes go on the wire.

## What would settle it

The three transformations are backed by a `ZoomData` structure that the assemblies' **metadata** names outright (reading names/attributes is within the rules; I did not decompile IL). Both `Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.dll` and `..._P20_IP.dll` contain the identifiers `ZoomData`, `ZoomDataTables`, `_zoomDataDictionary`, `TryGetZoomDataTable`, `Levels`, `Positions`, `PositionMinOptical`, `PositionMaxOptical`, `PositionStepOptical`, `LinearInterpolation`, `Ceiling`, `Floor`, `Round`. That corroborates the interpolation *shape* (linear over parallel `Levels[]`/`Positions[]` arrays, per model) and strongly suggests `ApplyZoomPositionStep` snaps to a `PositionStepOptical` grid with `Round`/`Ceiling`/`Floor` selected by mode. It does **not** give the array contents, and cannot tell me whether `Levels[]` is the 12/20 published rows or a denser sampling — which is precisely where the 11.8-vs-12 contradiction lives.

Settling it requires one of: (a) reading the RVA-initialised static array data for `Levels`/`Positions`/`PositionStepOptical` out of the assemblies' data section — data, not IL, but outside this experiment's brief; (b) a wire capture of a 4-Series control system driving a real I12/I20/P12/P20 through fractional zoom levels and across the digital boundary; (c) Crestron SDK source or a published `ZoomData` table.

## Does the fuller documentation change the "docs can't substitute for a shipped driver" finding?

It **reinforces it**, and now with numbers rather than assertion. The larger harvest did close one gap that was previously open — the optical anchor table and the ×16 digital limit are genuinely in the docs, and the docs alone get the 20x optical byte stream to within an interpolation-rule choice. But on this same expanded evidence base the documentation is now *demonstrably* wrong or silent about driver-visible values, in four independent places:

- Horizontal FOV: docs 67.68° / 56.45°, driver `Rules[30]/[31]` 67.0709° / 56.6965°.
- Optical top of the 12x level scale: docs 12x, driver's `ZoomLevel.Max = 188.8` implies 11.8x.
- Zoom position domain: docs describe only `0x0000`–`0x4000`, driver `Controllers[35] ZoomPosition.Max = 31424` (`0x7AC0`).
- The 32 FOV polynomial coefficients at 16 significant digits (`Controllers[34]`) and the focus-position bounds `15084/20664` and `12224/17114` in `Rules[30]/[31]` have no documentary counterpart at all.

Those four happen to be *declarative*, so possessing the shipped driver hands them over for free. The zoom `Levels`/`Positions`/`PositionStepOptical` arrays are the same species of calibration data — and they are the ones Crestron compiled. That asymmetry is the whole finding: documentation describes the device, the driver encodes the vendor's decisions about the device, and only the latter determines the bytes. Two of the three zoom transformations came back FAILED on the best documentation set that exists for these cameras.
